item.title: EYE NEWS UPDATE: All landlords ordered to register properties under new national scheme
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Landlords across England will need to register all rental properties under a forthcoming national scheme set to launch in December 2026, according to a government announcement. The mandatory registration system aims to improve oversight of the private rental sector, with phased regional implementation planned over the following year.

New registration requirements for landlords

The "Register your rental property" initiative will first roll out in the West Midlands before expanding nationwide. Landlords will have a three-month window to comply once their local area joins the scheme, with full implementation expected by November 2027. The annual registration fee has been set at £65 per property, renewable each year.

Initially targeting currently let properties and those becoming occupied during the rollout, the scheme will later extend to vacant rentals. Future legislation will require landlords to register empty properties before marketing them to tenants. Both landlords and letting agents must display registration numbers on all property advertisements.

Financial penalties await those who fail to register, with local councils gaining access to the database to identify non-compliant landlords. The government also plans to give tenants access to verify their landlord's registration status before committing to a tenancy.

Part of wider rental reforms

This registration service forms the foundation for a comprehensive national database of private rented properties. Housing Minister Matthew Pennycook described it as "an important first step" towards implementing the government's Renters' Rights Act, designed to empower tenants while supporting responsible landlords.

In related changes, the government has announced reforms to rent increase challenges. Responsibility for initial decisions will transfer from the First-tier Tribunal to HMRC's Valuation Office, potentially streamlining the process for tenants contesting rental hikes.

The combined measures represent significant changes to England's rental landscape, with implications for landlords, letting agents and tenants alike. Property investors may wish to review their portfolio management processes in preparation for these upcoming requirements.

item.title: Low-deposit mortgage lending hits 18-year high
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The proportion of low-deposit mortgages has reached its highest level in nearly two decades, as more homebuyers turn to higher loan-to-value (LTV) products to get onto the property ladder. According to the latest Bank of England data, 8.4% of gross mortgage advances in Q2 2026 were at 90% LTV or higher – marking the highest share since 2008.

Why low-deposit mortgages are gaining popularity

With house prices remaining elevated in many parts of the UK, prospective buyers are increasingly relying on mortgages requiring smaller deposits. The current 8.4% figure represents a notable increase from 7% during the same period last year, highlighting how vital these products have become for first-time buyers and those struggling to save substantial deposits.

Rachel Springall, a finance expert at Moneyfactscompare.co.uk, noted: "Saving for a large house deposit remains a significant challenge, particularly amidst the current cost-of-living pressures. Lenders have responded by offering more competitive products at higher LTV tiers, though borrowers should carefully consider their long-term affordability."

Those considering high LTV mortgages may wish to be mindful of potential risks such as negative equity should property values decline. Seeking independent financial advice and considering overpayments when possible could help mitigate these concerns.

Mortgage costs remain elevated

The Bank of England data also reveals ongoing pressure from higher borrowing costs. The proportion of mortgages priced 2-3 percentage points above the Base Rate rose to 3.1% in Q2 2026 – the highest level since early 2023.

Springall added: "With economists suggesting the Bank Rate could rise further rather than fall in the coming months, borrowers might not see relief from high mortgage rates anytime soon. It's worth remembering that fixed-rate mortgages follow swap rates rather than the Base Rate directly, adding another layer of complexity to rate predictions."

Homeowners approaching the end of their fixed-term deals may wish to explore their options well in advance, as shopping around could help secure more favourable terms.

Arrears show modest improvement

In more positive news, mortgage arrears have shown a slight improvement. The value of outstanding balances in arrears fell by 1.9% during the quarter to £19.7bn – the lowest figure since Q3 2023. The proportion of total mortgage balances in arrears remained steady at 1.1%.

This suggests that while higher interest rates continue to put pressure on household budgets, most borrowers are managing to keep up with repayments. However, experts caution that financial challenges persist for some households, particularly those on variable rate mortgages.

As the mortgage landscape evolves, staying informed about market trends and seeking professional advice could help borrowers make decisions suited to their individual circumstances.

item.title: Letting agents call for greater clarity over rent tribunals
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

As the rental sector adapts to the Renters’ Rights Act, industry experts are calling for improved clarity around rent tribunal processes. Propertymark, the professional body for property agents, highlights the need for simpler guidance and better support for both landlords and tenants navigating the First-tier Tribunal system.

Demands for clearer tribunal processes

The newly implemented rules require landlords in England to follow the Section 13 procedure when increasing rents for periodic tenancies, providing tenants with at least two months' notice. However, concerns have been raised about the complexity of challenging these increases through the tribunal system.

Greg Tsuman, former ARLA Propertymark president, emphasised the importance of accessible information: "We need much clearer guidance, simplified forms and practical advice for tenants considering challenging rent rises before they take effect." He also noted the tribunal's focus on actual achieved rents rather than advertised prices – a crucial distinction that both parties should understand.

Additional improvements suggested include enhancing the tribunal helpline service with properly trained staff capable of offering accurate legal guidance. These changes could help prevent unnecessary tribunal cases by ensuring both landlords and tenants better comprehend their rights and obligations.

The value of early intervention

Propertymark is encouraging letting agents to initiate affordability discussions with tenants before landlords serve Section 13 notices. Current president Kim Lidbury explained how proactive conversations could resolve issues before they escalate: "Tenants sometimes use rent increase notices to raise unrelated concerns, or may not disclose their full circumstances. Early dialogue could prevent unnecessary tribunal applications."

Maintaining tenancies benefits all parties, Lidbury added: "Most landlords have ongoing costs and responsibilities, while tenants benefit from stability. Prolonged occupancy generally represents the best outcome for both sides."

Tsuman reinforced that negotiation often presents a preferable alternative to formal proceedings: "Legislation doesn't prevent landlords and tenants from reaching mutual agreements outside the tribunal system. In many cases, constructive discussions can avoid the time and expense of legal processes."

The agent's role in dispute resolution

Letting agents can play a pivotal part in facilitating these discussions, helping landlords set reasonable rent increases while ensuring tenants' concerns are properly addressed. Propertymark suggests this mediation could reduce tribunal cases while maintaining fair outcomes for both parties.

As the rental market continues to adapt to legislative changes, clearer processes and improved communication channels may help create a more efficient system for handling rent disputes – ultimately benefiting landlords, tenants and letting professionals alike.

item.title: Renters squeezed as asking rents outstrip budgets
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

New research highlights the growing financial strain on UK renters, with nearly 40% now spending over half their income on rent alone. Data from flatshare platform SpareRoom reveals a widening gap between what tenants can afford and what landlords are asking, forcing many to make difficult housing decisions.

Rent costs outpace tenant budgets

SpareRoom's analysis of Q2 2026 data shows average room rents exceeded tenants' budgets in half of the 35 major cities surveyed. The situation appears most severe in Edinburgh, where the average £834 monthly room rent sits £86 above typical renter budgets - an annual shortfall exceeding £1,000. York and Derby follow closely, with yearly affordability gaps of £611 and £607 respectively.

The research identified several other cities where rental prices consistently outstrip what flatsharers can pay:

  • Belfast (£38 monthly gap)
  • Glasgow (£36 monthly gap)
  • Cardiff (£35 monthly gap)
  • Birmingham (£29 monthly gap)

Financial pressure forcing moves

The affordability crisis is having real-world consequences, with SpareRoom's July 2026 survey revealing 32% of UK renters had been compelled to relocate in the past year due to unaffordable rents. Traditional budgeting advice suggesting housing costs shouldn't exceed 30% of income now seems unrealistic for many, with just 15.3% of renters achieving this benchmark.

By contrast, 37.8% of respondents reported spending over half their income on rent (excluding bills) - a situation that leaves little room for other essential expenses or savings. This financial squeeze may explain why increasing numbers of renters are considering alternative options, including moving to cheaper areas or exploring shared accommodation.

For those struggling with rental costs, it could be worth reviewing all available housing options. Some renters might consider negotiating longer tenancies in exchange for fixed rental rates, while others may wish to explore whether they could potentially transition to homeownership with current government support schemes.

item.title: Agents offered free AML guidance as regulations change
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Property professionals across the UK now have access to free anti-money laundering (AML) guidance as regulatory updates come into effect. AML compliance specialists FCS Compliance are hosting an interactive webinar on 23rd September to help estate agents, letting agents and property professionals navigate the recent changes.

Understanding the regulatory updates

The upcoming webinar will focus on recent amendments to the Money Laundering Regulations (MLRs) and revised guidance from HMRC. These changes represent some of the most substantial updates to the AML framework affecting the property sector in recent years. Industry professionals may find it valuable to familiarise themselves with the new requirements, which could impact their daily operations and compliance procedures.

The session follows a previous event hosted by FCS Compliance, which reportedly generated numerous follow-up enquiries from attendees. Many questions centred on practical implementation of the regulatory changes within property businesses. The new webinar aims to address these queries directly, providing clarity on how to apply the updated rules in real-world scenarios.

Expert-led compliance guidance

Stephen Williamson, lead AML consultant at FCS Compliance, will host the event alongside senior consultant Jen Siwicki. Williamson noted: "The property sector is facing significant changes to its AML obligations. This webinar offers professionals the chance to have their specific questions answered by compliance specialists."

The hour-long session is scheduled for 1pm and will adopt an interactive format, with emphasis on answering participants' questions. Property professionals might consider attending to ensure their businesses remain fully compliant with the updated regulations. Topics will likely cover customer due diligence requirements, risk assessments and reporting obligations under the revised framework.

For those unable to attend live, it could be worth contacting FCS Compliance directly for information about future sessions or recorded materials. Staying informed about AML requirements helps property businesses avoid potential penalties whilst maintaining professional standards in this heavily regulated sector.

item.title: Lettings portfolios become hot property in estate agency acquisition race
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The UK estate agency sector is undergoing a significant transformation, with lettings portfolios becoming a prime focus for acquisition activity. According to research by The Business Acquisitions Group (BAG), buyers are increasingly prioritising recurring managed lettings income over acquiring entire agencies. This trend reflects a broader shift in the market, driven by private equity-backed businesses and evolving buyer strategies.

Why Lettings Portfolios Are in Demand

Managed lettings portfolios offer a steady stream of income, making them an attractive proposition for buyers. Unlike sales income, which can fluctuate with market conditions, lettings provide consistent revenue. This stability is particularly appealing in uncertain economic times. Recent examples include Lomond’s acquisition of Edward Mellor’s lettings division and Dwelly’s purchase of AP Morgan’s lettings business, both highlighting this growing trend.

Martin Bunney, founder and managing director of BAG, notes that buyers are increasingly assessing the sales and lettings elements of agencies separately. “Sales income is welcome, but all serious buyers are now competing for managed income,” he explains. For sellers, ensuring their lettings portfolio is well-maintained and organised could enhance its appeal to potential buyers.

The Role of Private Equity in Consolidation

Private equity-backed platforms are playing an increasingly prominent role in the acquisition market. These platforms are often well-funded and strategically focused on building substantial lettings portfolios. Campions Group, the UK arm of French group Emeria, is one such active buyer, particularly in London.

New sources of acquisition finance are also broadening the pool of potential purchasers. For example, property investment business Sourced launched a programme in 2025 offering franchisees funding to acquire letting agencies. This development has further intensified competition in the market.

Implications for Estate Agency Owners

For owners of combined sales and lettings agencies, this shift in buyer focus could influence their exit strategies. Bunney observes that the acquisition market has evolved, with buyer strategy moving away from entire agencies by large franchise groups to lettings books by private equity platforms. This change may prompt agency owners to consider separating their sales and lettings businesses to maximise their value.

The research by BAG underscores the importance of understanding these market dynamics. With lettings portfolios now a hot commodity, agency owners might wish to evaluate their options carefully, particularly if they are considering selling. Ensuring their lettings business is in good shape could make it a more attractive proposition in this competitive landscape.

As the estate agency sector continues to consolidate, lettings portfolios are likely to remain a key focus for buyers. With private equity-backed platforms driving much of this activity, the market is set to evolve further in the coming years.

item.title: Estate agents not to blame for property sale delays – Rightmove
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

When it comes to property transactions, delays can be frustrating for all parties involved. However, recent research from Rightmove suggests that estate agents are often unfairly blamed for these hold-ups. In reality, the majority of delays stem from other stages of the process, many of which are beyond an estate agent’s control. Understanding these factors could help homeowners better navigate the complexities of buying and selling property.

Where Do Delays Occur?

According to Rightmove’s findings, conveyancing is the most common source of delays, cited by 37% of home movers. This legal process, which involves transferring property ownership, can be time-consuming and often depends on external parties such as solicitors. Additionally, 15% of respondents highlighted survey or valuation issues as a cause of delays, while 11% pointed to problems with property searches. A further 11% experienced setbacks when another party withdrew from the transaction and needed to be replaced, and 9% attributed delays to chain-related complications. By comparison, only 5% of respondents identified poor buyer qualification as a factor.

The Role of Estate Agents

The research underscores the importance of recognising the role estate agents play in facilitating property transactions. While their work is often behind the scenes, they play a vital part in coordinating various stages of the process. Christian Balshen, director of agency partnerships at Rightmove, emphasised that many delays occur outside of agents’ direct control. He noted, “The work estate agents do is often underestimated because much of what they deliver happens behind the scenes. We want to help the public better understand the value agents provide.”

Improving the Home Moving Process

Rightmove is actively working to improve consumer understanding of the property transaction process. The company has launched a home mover education programme, which draws on insights from independent agents to provide guidance to buyers and sellers. Additionally, Rightmove has been hosting webinars and events with industry figures to discuss ways to speed up transactions and reduce fall-through rates. This initiative aligns with the government’s Home Buying and Selling Reform Roadmap, which aims to streamline the process for all parties involved.

For those considering a move, it could be worth taking the time to understand the various stages of the transaction process. Estate agents play a crucial role, but delays can arise from multiple sources. By staying informed and prepared, homeowners may find the journey to their new property smoother and less stressful.

item.title: Estate agents pull ‘unsellable’ leasehold properties from market
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Leasehold properties are increasingly becoming a challenge to sell, with new research revealing that over three-quarters of estate agents have withdrawn such homes from the market due to their unsellable nature. According to Propertymark, 78% of agents have taken this step, whilst less than 1% reported that selling leasehold properties has become easier in the last two years. The trade body is urging the government to expedite leasehold reforms to better protect existing homeowners as the market transitions towards commonhold.

The Growing Challenges of Leasehold Properties

The research, based on responses from over 1,200 leaseholders and 200 Propertymark members, paints a concerning picture. A staggering 93% of leaseholders stated they would not purchase a leasehold property again, citing issues such as escalating service charges and difficulties in challenging unfair fees. Service charges, in particular, have emerged as a significant barrier to sales, with 74% of agents identifying them as a major obstacle. Some reported cases where annual charges doubled from £1,000-£2,000 to £3,000-£4,000, raising affordability concerns for potential buyers and even affecting mortgage eligibility.

Delays in obtaining necessary information for leasehold transactions further complicate the process. Around 40% of agents noted that securing the required details can take more than 15 days, sometimes stretching to several months. Only 17% typically receive the information within five days. These delays can frustrate buyers and sellers alike, adding to the already complex nature of leasehold transactions.

Building Safety Concerns and the Need for Reform

Building safety defects continue to cast a shadow over leasehold properties, further hindering sales. Propertymark’s analysis highlights the ongoing impact of these issues, particularly in England, where remediation efforts for affected flats are still underway. The combination of rising service charges, building safety concerns, and bureaucratic delays has left many leaseholders in a difficult position, with some finding their properties effectively unsellable.

Timothy Douglas, Head of Policy and Campaigns at Propertymark, emphasised the urgency of reform. He noted that whilst the move towards commonhold is welcome, existing leaseholders cannot afford to wait decades for change. Immediate action is needed to address unaffordable service charges, building safety problems, and the broader challenges faced by homeowners. Douglas called on the UK government to act swiftly to restore confidence in the market and provide much-needed support to leaseholders and property professionals.

As the leasehold system faces mounting criticism, homeowners may wish to carefully consider their options when buying or selling leasehold properties. Whilst reforms are on the horizon, the current challenges highlight the importance of understanding the implications of leasehold ownership and staying informed about potential changes in legislation.

By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Leasehold properties are increasingly becoming a challenge to sell, with new research revealing that over three-quarters of estate agents have withdrawn such homes from the market due to their unsellable nature. According to Propertymark, 78% of agents have taken this step, whilst less than 1% reported that selling leasehold properties has become easier in the last two years. The trade body is urging the government to expedite leasehold reforms to better protect existing homeowners as the market transitions towards commonhold.

The Growing Challenges of Leasehold Properties

The research, based on responses from over 1,200 leaseholders and 200 Propertymark members, paints a concerning picture. A staggering 93% of leaseholders stated they would not purchase a leasehold property again, citing issues such as escalating service charges and difficulties in challenging unfair fees. Service charges, in particular, have emerged as a significant barrier to sales, with 74% of agents identifying them as a major obstacle. Some reported cases where annual charges doubled from £1,000-£2,000 to £3,000-£4,000, raising affordability concerns for potential buyers and even affecting mortgage eligibility.

Delays in obtaining necessary information for leasehold transactions further complicate the process. Around 40% of agents noted that securing the required details can take more than 15 days, sometimes stretching to several months. Only 17% typically receive the information within five days. These delays can frustrate buyers and sellers alike, adding to the already complex nature of leasehold transactions.

Building Safety Concerns and the Need for Reform

Building safety defects continue to cast a shadow over leasehold properties, further hindering sales. Propertymark’s analysis highlights the ongoing impact of these issues, particularly in England, where remediation efforts for affected flats are still underway. The combination of rising service charges, building safety concerns, and bureaucratic delays has left many leaseholders in a difficult position, with some finding their properties effectively unsellable.

Timothy Douglas, Head of Policy and Campaigns at Propertymark, emphasised the urgency of reform. He noted that whilst the move towards commonhold is welcome, existing leaseholders cannot afford to wait decades for change. Immediate action is needed to address unaffordable service charges, building safety problems, and the broader challenges faced by homeowners. Douglas called on the UK government to act swiftly to restore confidence in the market and provide much-needed support to leaseholders and property professionals.

As the leasehold system faces mounting criticism, homeowners may wish to carefully consider their options when buying or selling leasehold properties. Whilst reforms are on the horizon, the current challenges highlight the importance of understanding the implications of leasehold ownership and staying informed about potential changes in legislation.

item.title: Letting agents face £40,000 penalties as licensing rules expand
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

Letting agents and landlords across England could face penalties of up to £40,000 for licensing breaches as local authorities expand regulation in the private rented sector. With councils introducing new selective and additional licensing schemes, industry body Propertymark is urging property professionals to stay informed about local requirements.

Higher penalties now in force

The first phase of the Renters' Rights Act, which came into effect on 1st May 2026, has increased the maximum civil penalty for Housing Act offences from £30,000 to £40,000. Councils can now impose these substantial fines for offences including operating a House in Multiple Occupation (HMO) without the required licence or breaching licence conditions. The changes form part of a broader trend towards stricter enforcement in the private rental market.

Growing complexity in licensing requirements

Local authorities across England are currently considering new or expanded licensing schemes, with some councils also exploring Article 4 Directions affecting HMOs. Propertymark highlights how these local regulations, combined with higher penalties, have created an increasingly complex compliance landscape for agents and landlords.

Operating an unlicensed property carries multiple risks beyond civil penalties. Those managing properties may face liability, and landlords in rent-to-rent arrangements could find themselves responsible for compliance failures. In some cases, councils and tenants may pursue rent repayment orders, potentially reclaiming up to two years' rent where proper licensing hasn't been obtained.

Industry calls for proportionate regulation

Tim Thomas of Propertymark commented: "The regulatory landscape for the private rented sector is becoming increasingly complex, with rising costs for compliance failures. It's essential that agents and landlords fully understand licensing requirements, applicable conditions and responsibilities within property ownership structures."

While acknowledging licensing's role in maintaining standards, Propertymark advocates for evidence-based schemes that avoid unnecessary bureaucracy. The organisation stresses that responsible landlords and professional agents should not be hindered by excessive administration or inconsistent local requirements that could limit housing supply.

Looking ahead, the planned Private Rented Sector Database, set for regional rollout from late 2026, will introduce another compliance layer. While supporting the principle of a national register, Propertymark emphasises the need for better coordination between different regulatory systems to avoid duplicating requirements for compliant operators.

For landlords and agents, staying informed about local licensing schemes and maintaining up-to-date records has become more crucial than ever. With financial penalties increasing and new regulations emerging, thorough due diligence could help property professionals navigate this evolving landscape.

item.title: Comings & Goings
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The UK property and mortgage sectors are witnessing notable shifts as industry professionals make strategic career moves. From high-profile departures to key appointments, these changes highlight evolving trends in the market, particularly the growing appeal of self-employed brokerage models and the strengthening of leadership teams in established agencies.

Senior Director Joins Moveli After Two Decades at Savills

David Johnston, a seasoned estate agent with over 23 years of experience, has left Savills after 21 years to join Moveli, a self-employed brokerage firm. Johnston, who previously served as a director in Savills’ country sales team in Sevenoaks, brings extensive knowledge of the local market to his new role. His departure marks a significant shift from the traditional agency model to the increasingly popular self-employed approach.

Moveli, which focuses on the upper end of the residential market, has seen rapid growth in recent years. According to TwentyEA data, self-employed agents now account for 2.5% of the UK residential market share, representing an 18.6% increase compared to 2025. The firm boasts a network of over 100 agents and continues to invest heavily in proprietary technology to enhance its offerings.

Ben Littlewood, co-founder of Moveli, commented on Johnston’s appointment, stating, “David is an exceptional agent, and his move to Moveli speaks volumes about the changing market dynamics and the strength of our brand. We anticipate further growth and success as we attract more high-calibre brokers and expand our presence in the upper market.”

Landstones Strengthens Leadership Team

In another significant development, South West London estate agency Landstones has appointed Mo Kanso as its managing director. Kanso brings a wealth of experience from the residential property sector, including a previous role at Draker Lettings, where he played a key role in expanding the firm’s lettings department and opening new offices.

At Landstones, Kanso will focus on enhancing the agency’s presence across its core markets, with particular emphasis on SW6. He noted, “SW6 is a crucial market for us, and Landstones has consistently performed well in this area. I look forward to driving further growth and strengthening our position in the region.”

Expertise Added to Norton Rose Fulbright

Meanwhile, global law firm Norton Rose Fulbright has bolstered its real estate team with the appointment of Simon Woodcock as a partner. Woodcock’s extensive expertise in property law is expected to further enhance the firm’s capabilities in handling complex real estate transactions and advising clients in the sector.

These appointments and career moves underscore the dynamic nature of the UK property and mortgage markets. As professionals adapt to evolving trends and new opportunities, their contributions are likely to shape the future of the industry.

For homeowners and property investors, staying informed about these developments could provide valuable insights into market trends and the expertise available to support their decisions.

item.title: Fresh mortgage rate rises threaten autumn housing market
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Homeowners and prospective buyers may face fresh challenges in the coming weeks as major lenders increase mortgage rates in response to rising swap rates. HSBC, Barclays and NatWest are among the high-street banks to have adjusted their pricing since the start of September, with further rises expected across the market. This development could impact buyer affordability and dampen activity in the autumn housing market, which is typically a busy period for estate agents.

What’s Driving Mortgage Rate Increases?

Mortgage lenders often base their fixed-rate deals on swap rates, which reflect the cost of borrowing in the financial markets. Recent volatility in these rates has prompted banks and building societies to review their pricing. Whilst lenders have responded cautiously compared to earlier in the year, the upward trend in swap rates has led to noticeable adjustments. For example, a 0.25 percentage point increase on a £250,000 mortgage could add around £38 to monthly repayments, equating to an extra £456 annually over a 25-year term.

Rachel Springall, a finance expert at Moneyfactscompare.co.uk, commented: “The pricing margins among major lenders are under pressure due to renewed volatility in the swap rate market. It’s somewhat inevitable for them to adjust rates, and we’ve already seen moves from HSBC and NatWest since the start of September.”

What Does This Mean for the Housing Market?

Higher mortgage rates could reduce borrowing power and affordability for buyers, potentially impacting transaction volumes and budgets. Even modest rate increases may deter some prospective homeowners, particularly first-time buyers or those on tighter finances. Estate agents will be closely monitoring the situation, as any slowdown in buyer activity could affect agreed sales and market momentum during the autumn period.

Unlike the rapid repricing seen earlier in the year, lenders have been more measured in their response so far. However, some, such as the Family Building Society, have temporarily withdrawn fixed-rate products. This cautious approach suggests lenders are balancing rising costs with the need to remain competitive in the market.

For homeowners approaching the end of their fixed-rate deals, it could be worth exploring remortgage options sooner rather than later to lock in competitive rates. Borrowers might also consider seeking advice from a mortgage broker to navigate the changing landscape and find a deal that suits their circumstances.

As the market evolves, keeping a close eye on lender announcements and rate changes will be crucial for anyone planning to buy or remortgage in the near future.

item.title: Landlord possession claims surge after Renters’ Rights shake-up
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The introduction of the Renters’ Rights Act has led to a notable rise in landlord possession claims across the UK. According to recent government figures, accelerated possession claims increased by 16% between April and June 2026 compared to the same period last year. This surge reflects the ongoing adjustments within the private rented sector following the Act’s implementation in May 2026, which abolished Section 21 ‘no-fault’ evictions.

Impact of the Renters’ Rights Act

The Renters’ Rights Act, effective from 1 May 2026, has brought significant changes to the private rental market. One of its key provisions was the removal of Section 21 notices, which previously allowed landlords to evict tenants without providing a reason. In anticipation of this change, many landlords rushed to serve Section 21 notices before the deadline, leading to a spike in possession claims. However, tenants facing eviction have increasingly contested these notices, resulting in prolonged legal disputes.

Law firms, such as Thackray Williams in the South East, have reported a sharp rise in instructions from both landlords seeking vacant possession and tenants challenging eviction notices. Mustafa Sidki, a partner at the firm, highlighted that these disputes often require full court hearings, increasing costs for landlords and leaving tenants in a state of uncertainty. He also noted that tenants frequently request additional time from courts to find alternative accommodation, further delaying the process.

Landlords Exiting the Market

Separate research suggests that some landlords are choosing to reduce their exposure to the private rented sector altogether. A Savills survey conducted in June 2026 found that 11% of landlords had sold one or more properties. This trend is exacerbating the shortage of affordable rental housing, making it even more challenging for tenants to find suitable accommodation.

Sidki explained that the combination of landlords exiting the market and tenants resisting eviction is creating a “perfect storm” within the sector. He warned that unless more affordable rental homes become available and the economics of the private rented sector improve, both landlords and tenants will continue to face significant challenges. Landlords may encounter rising costs as tenants contest evictions, while renters struggle to secure housing amidst dwindling options.

The ongoing disputes are also placing additional pressure on the court system, which is already grappling with a growing backlog of cases. As landlords and tenants navigate these complexities, it could be worth seeking professional advice to understand their rights and responsibilities under the new legislation.

In summary, the Renters’ Rights Act has sparked a wave of possession claims and legal disputes within the private rented sector. With landlords reducing their portfolios and tenants facing difficulties finding alternative accommodation, the market is experiencing heightened tensions. Both parties may wish to stay informed about their legal options to navigate this evolving landscape effectively.

item.title: Comings & Goings
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

The UK property and mortgage sectors have seen some notable career moves recently, with experienced professionals taking on fresh challenges in their fields. From transitioning to self-employed brokerage models to returning to familiar roles with new responsibilities, these changes highlight the evolving landscape of the industry.

From Foxtons to Harding Green: A New Chapter for Jas Dhaliwal

Jas Dhaliwal, a seasoned professional with 17 years of experience at Foxtons, has made a significant career shift by joining Harding Green as a partner. During his tenure at Foxtons, Dhaliwal held key roles, including operations director at the agency’s Sloane Square and Shepherd’s Bush offices. His move to Harding Green marks a transition from a traditional agency environment to a self-employed broker model.

Dhaliwal expressed his enthusiasm for the new role, stating, “After 17 years at Foxtons, it felt like the right time for a new challenge. I’m delighted to have joined Nick and the team at Harding Green as a partner.” He believes the self-employed model represents the future of the industry, offering experienced agents the chance to provide a more personalised and focused service. Nick Carter, CEO of Harding Green, welcomed Dhaliwal, highlighting the rarity of finding someone with such extensive experience at a single company.

Ron Cole’s Return to Spicerhaart

In another notable career move, Ron Cole, a former Army paratrooper and Strongman champion, has returned to Spicerhaart as an area director for haart estate agents. Cole, who previously worked with Spicerhaart between 2009 and 2013, brings 27 years of estate agency experience to his new role. He will oversee operations across Middlesex and North London, focusing on managing and developing teams in the region.

Cole shared his excitement about the opportunity, saying, “I’m thrilled by the chance to coach and develop a larger team across a wider region. That’s exactly what motivates me now.” He emphasised the importance of building people up and creating a positive environment where individuals can achieve more than they thought possible. Outside of estate agency, Cole’s background includes serving in the Parachute Regiment and competing in Strongman events, where he became champion for Watford and Hertfordshire.

Keiron Humphreys, managing director of one of Spicerhaart’s estate agency divisions, praised Cole’s exceptional track record and leadership qualities, noting that his return is a valuable addition to the team.

These career moves underscore the dynamic nature of the UK property and mortgage sectors, with experienced professionals embracing new challenges and opportunities. Their transitions reflect broader trends in the industry, including the rise of self-employed brokerage models and the importance of strong leadership in team development.

item.title: Better mortgage deals drive borrowers to switch banks
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

With mortgage rates continuing to shape the property market, many borrowers are exploring ways to reduce the cost of moving home. Recent research highlights that switching banks to secure better mortgage deals has become a key consideration for homeowners, particularly as affordability pressures persist. Understanding how mortgage rates and incentives influence financial decisions could help borrowers make more informed choices.

Why Borrowers Are Switching Banks

The study, which surveyed 2,000 UK adults who had moved home in the last two years, found that 41% of mortgage holders switched banks to access more competitive mortgage deals. A further 30% were motivated by mortgage-linked incentives, while 28% sought higher interest rates on their savings. These findings underscore the significance of mortgage costs in moving decisions, as even small changes in rates can impact monthly repayments and borrowing capacity.

Despite this focus on mortgage rates, switching banks during a home move remains relatively uncommon. Only 15% of movers changed their bank account, compared to higher switching rates in other areas such as broadband (46%), energy suppliers (38%), and mobile phone providers (35%). Interestingly, 58% of movers did not review or consider switching their bank account, with nearly a third unaware that it could be a worthwhile option.

Research Habits Among Home Movers

The research also revealed how home movers allocate their time when preparing for a move. Half of respondents investigated local property prices, while 48% looked into energy suppliers and broadband providers. However, just 22% explored current accounts or alternative banking options. This suggests that whilst borrowers are keen to reduce costs, banking arrangements are often overlooked during the moving process.

For those considering a switch, it could be worth comparing bank accounts and mortgage deals alongside other moving expenses. Checking for competitive rates, incentives, and savings options might help homeowners optimise their finances during a property transaction.

Age Differences in Switching Behaviour

Age played a significant role in whether movers considered changing their bank account. Half of 18 to 24-year-olds reviewed or switched their current account, with the figure rising slightly to 51% among those aged 25 to 34. However, this trend declined with age, falling to 30% for 45 to 54-year-olds and just 19% for those over 55. Younger movers were also more likely to follow through with a switch, with 22% of 18 to 24-year-olds changing their bank account compared to only 8% of over-55s.

As affordability remains a central concern for home movers, borrowers may wish to look beyond property prices alone. Considering mortgage rates, banking options, and incentives could help reduce the overall cost of moving. With younger generations more likely to explore these avenues, there may be opportunities for all homeowners to reassess their financial arrangements during a property transaction.

item.title: Gross rental income rises to £90,000 for average landlord
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Landlords across the UK have seen their gross rental incomes rise substantially, with recent data suggesting the average property investor now earns approximately £90,000 annually from lettings. Whilst this marks a significant increase in revenue streams, industry analysts note that operating costs and mortgage expenses have also climbed, potentially affecting net profitability.

Rental market shows resilience despite economic pressures

The private rental sector continues to demonstrate strength, with gross yields growing as demand outstrips supply in many regions. Several factors contribute to this trend, including population growth, delayed first-time buyer purchases, and limited new housing stock. Landlords with multiple properties may find their combined rental income reaching the £90,000 average as market conditions favour established investors.

However, property owners should be aware that gross income figures don't reflect the full financial picture. Rising interest rates have increased mortgage repayments for those with variable or tracker deals, whilst maintenance costs and regulatory compliance expenses have similarly grown. Some buy-to-let investors might need to reassess their portfolios to maintain healthy profit margins.

Important considerations for landlords

For those evaluating their property investments, several key aspects warrant attention:

  • Tax implications: Higher rental income may push some landlords into different tax brackets, affecting overall profitability
  • Mortgage options: Remortgaging could help secure better rates amidst changing market conditions
  • Energy efficiency requirements: Upcoming EPC regulations may necessitate property upgrades
  • Insurance costs: Comprehensive landlord cover remains essential as premiums adjust to inflation

Professional property management services might appeal to investors seeking to streamline operations, though this comes at an additional cost that affects net returns. Portfolio landlords with multiple properties might consider diversifying their holdings across different regions to mitigate local market risks.

Whilst rising gross incomes present opportunities, prudent landlords will balance these against increasing outgoings to maintain sustainable rental businesses. Financial advice tailored to individual circumstances could prove valuable in navigating this complex landscape.

item.title: Fall in mortgage approvals reflects July price volatility
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Mortgage approvals experienced a noticeable dip in July, as fluctuating interest rates and economic uncertainty impacted buyer confidence and affordability. This downturn reflects the broader volatility in the property market, with potential homeowners and investors adopting a more cautious approach amidst the unpredictable financial landscape.

Impact of Rate Uncertainty on Mortgage Activity

The decline in mortgage approvals can be largely attributed to the ongoing uncertainty surrounding interest rates. With the Bank of England's base rate adjustments and lenders frequently revising their mortgage products, many borrowers may have paused their plans to secure a home loan. This hesitation is understandable, as rate changes can significantly affect monthly repayments and overall affordability.

First-time buyers and those looking to remortgage may have found themselves particularly vulnerable to these shifts. The fluctuating rates could have made it challenging to lock in a favourable deal, prompting some to delay their decisions until the market stabilises.

Affordability Concerns and Buyer Confidence

Affordability remains a key concern for many prospective homeowners, especially in light of rising living costs and inflation. The combination of higher mortgage rates and increased household expenses has placed additional financial pressure on buyers, leading to a more cautious approach to property purchases.

For those considering stepping onto the property ladder, the current climate may feel particularly daunting. The uncertainty surrounding future rate changes and the potential for further economic instability could be discouraging some from taking the plunge. Similarly, homeowners looking to remortgage might be weighing their options carefully, seeking to balance affordability with long-term financial security.

Looking Ahead: What Borrowers Might Consider

Whilst the current market presents challenges, there are steps borrowers might consider to navigate the volatility. Seeking advice from a mortgage broker could help identify the most suitable options based on individual circumstances. Additionally, keeping a close eye on rate trends and lender offers may enable borrowers to secure a competitive deal when the time is right.

For those able to proceed, fixed-rate mortgages could offer a sense of stability amidst the uncertainty. Locking in a rate for a set period might provide peace of mind, shielding borrowers from potential rate hikes in the near future.

As the property market continues to evolve, staying informed and seeking professional guidance could prove invaluable for those looking to make confident, well-informed decisions.

item.title: House prices down second month in a row
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

UK house prices have fallen for two consecutive months according to latest industry data, as affordability constraints and higher mortgage costs continue to impact buyer demand. The figures from Lloyds Banking Group suggest a cautious market sentiment amongst prospective purchasers facing ongoing financial pressures.

What the latest house price data shows

The recent dip marks the first back-to-back monthly decline in property values since early 2023, with analysts noting particular softening in regional markets outside London. Whilst annual growth remains positive across most areas, the monthly contraction indicates cooling demand as borrowers grapple with elevated interest rates and living costs.

Market observers highlight several factors influencing current conditions:

  • Mortgage rates remaining above 2021/2022 levels despite recent stabilisation
  • Ongoing affordability challenges for first-time buyers
  • Reduced buying power due to the cumulative effect of rising rates
  • Some homeowners choosing to delay moving plans

How this affects different market segments

The current conditions create varied impacts across different buyer groups. Existing homeowners with substantial equity may find they retain significant bargaining power, whilst first-time buyers continue facing deposit hurdles. Buy-to-let investors are reassessing yields as rental growth shows signs of slowing in some areas.

For those considering their next move, several approaches might be worth considering:

  • Monitoring local market trends rather than national averages
  • Seeking independent mortgage advice to understand borrowing capacity
  • Exploring different mortgage products that could suit changing circumstances
  • Being prepared for potentially longer sales completion timelines

As always in fluctuating markets, taking a measured approach and seeking professional financial guidance can help individuals make informed property decisions tailored to their personal circumstances.

item.title: Atom Bank launches funding for BNG habitat banks
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

Atom Bank has introduced a new lending initiative aimed at supporting habitat creation projects, which could assist property developers in meeting Biodiversity Net Gain (BNG) requirements. This move highlights the growing importance of sustainability and environmental considerations in the UK property and mortgage sectors.

What is Biodiversity Net Gain?

Biodiversity Net Gain is a policy introduced in England to ensure that development projects leave natural habitats in a better state than before. Under these regulations, developers are required to demonstrate a measurable increase in biodiversity, often achieved through habitat creation or enhancement. This approach aims to balance urban growth with environmental conservation, ensuring that wildlife and ecosystems are protected.

How Atom Bank’s Lending Initiative Works

Atom Bank’s new funding scheme focuses on providing financial support for habitat banks, which are areas designated for biodiversity enhancement. These habitat banks can help developers meet their BNG obligations by offsetting any ecological impact caused by their projects. By offering tailored financing solutions, Atom Bank aims to make it easier for developers to comply with environmental regulations whilst fostering sustainable development.

This initiative not only supports developers but also contributes to broader environmental goals. Habitat banks can play a crucial role in restoring natural landscapes, improving biodiversity, and mitigating the effects of climate change. For developers, access to such funding could streamline the planning process and reduce the complexity of meeting BNG requirements.

Why This Matters for the Property Sector

The introduction of this lending initiative reflects a broader trend in the property sector towards integrating environmental considerations into development projects. As sustainability becomes a key focus, developers and lenders alike are exploring innovative ways to align their activities with environmental goals. Atom Bank’s funding for habitat banks is an example of how financial institutions can play a role in promoting greener development practices.

For homeowners and property investors, this shift towards sustainable development could also have long-term benefits. Properties built with biodiversity in mind may appeal to environmentally conscious buyers and could potentially see increased demand in the future.

Atom Bank’s new lending initiative underscores the growing intersection of finance, property, and environmental sustainability. By supporting habitat creation and helping developers meet BNG requirements, this scheme highlights the importance of balancing economic growth with ecological preservation. Borrowers and developers alike might find value in exploring how such initiatives can support their goals whilst contributing to a greener future.

item.title: The growth of sustainable living and why successful investment starts with delivery
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The rise of sustainable living has become a significant trend in the UK property market, with homeowners increasingly prioritising eco-friendly features and energy-efficient homes. This shift reflects growing environmental awareness and the desire to reduce long-term living costs. However, for investors and developers, delivering sustainable properties that meet genuine demand requires careful planning, robust assets, and a commitment to long-term execution.

The appeal of sustainable living

Sustainable living is no longer a niche concept but a mainstream priority for many buyers and renters. Features such as solar panels, heat pumps, and improved insulation are becoming key selling points. Homeowners may find that investing in such properties not only aligns with their environmental values but also offers potential savings on utility bills. Additionally, government incentives and stricter energy efficiency regulations are further driving interest in eco-friendly homes.

Key factors for successful investment

For those considering investing in sustainable property, several factors could influence success. Firstly, understanding genuine market demand is crucial. Properties with sustainable features must cater to the needs and preferences of the target audience. Secondly, the quality of assets plays a vital role. High-performance materials and reliable eco-technologies can enhance a property’s appeal and longevity. Finally, effective delivery is essential. Projects must be completed on time and to a high standard to build trust and maximise returns.

The importance of long-term planning

Sustainable property investment often requires a forward-thinking approach. Developers and investors might consider the lifecycle of eco-friendly technologies and how they will perform over time. Regular maintenance and updates could be necessary to ensure properties remain efficient and attractive to future buyers or tenants. Long-term planning also involves staying informed about evolving regulations and technological advancements in the sustainable living sector.

As the demand for eco-friendly homes continues to grow, sustainable living presents both opportunities and challenges for the property market. By focusing on genuine demand, strong assets, and effective delivery, investors and homeowners alike could benefit from this burgeoning trend.
